summary: Describes a service URN to identify well-known services that depend on context, such as the user's location. Examples include emergency services, directory assistance, and call-before-you-dig lines. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A standard name for things like the emergency number that points to the nearest help.

questions: how to identify emergency services by urn
subtitle: A single global name for services like emergency help, resolved to a local provider wherever you are.

tldr.problem: Well-known services such as emergency help are reached by different numbers in different countries, and the same number can mean something else elsewhere. Travelers and devices made abroad struggle to reach them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5031 registers a URN namespace, urn:service:, whose hierarchical labels (such as sos.fire) name a kind of service. Separate resolution protocols map the name to a provider near the user.
tldr.outcome: It defines the sos and counseling top-level services and an IANA registry for more. RFC 7163 updates it.

today: RFC 5031 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7163; read the two together. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Service URN
sections.content:
Many well-known services are run by loosely coordinated local organizations but reached through a well-known identifier, such as 9-1-1 in North America or 1-1-2 in Europe. Almost all of these identifiers work only in one country or group of countries, and the same identifier is often used for something else elsewhere. That makes services hard to reach for travelers or for devices produced outside their home country.

The RFC proposes a URN namespace for such services. The identifier stays stable, the service is administered in a decentralized way, and resolution protocols outside this document map the identifier to a real provider. A device can then say which service it wants, and proxies can route the request without knowing every dial string in the world.
sections.eli5: Phone numbers for help differ from country to country. A single universal name for each kind of help means your phone can ask for "fire" anywhere and the network figures out who to call.

sections.title: How the URN Is Used
sections.content:
The service URN is a protocol element and is generally not expected to be visible to people. Callers still dial the local number, such as 9-1-1 in the United States. The end host translating dial strings into service URNs is out of scope, but several numbers may map to one URN: a traveler's phone could map both the home and the visited emergency numbers to urn:service:sos.

The URN can appear wherever general URIs are allowed, for example in a SIP request URI. Because service URNs are not routable, a SIP proxy or user agent has to translate the URN into a routable URI for a location-appropriate provider. The RFC expects the Location-to-Service Translation Protocol (LoST) to be used for this, and says several such protocols may exist, possibly different ones for different services. Speed dial buttons for emergency help are described as inappropriate by most emergency services professionals on mobile devices, because they are too easily triggered by accident.
sections.eli5: You still press the same buttons as always. Behind the scenes your phone swaps the number for a universal name, and the network turns that name into the nearest real helper.

sections.title: Syntax of Service URNs
sections.content:
Section 3 is the registration template required by RFC 3406. The namespace ID is service. A URN is a hierarchy of labels separated by periods. The left-most label is the top-level service and labels to its right are sub-services. Characters are those allowed in domain names. Labels are case-insensitive but MUST be written in lower case.

Labels can be removed from the right and the result is still valid: if x.y.z exists, so do x and x.y, each naming a more generic service. Comparison is case-insensitive string equality.

service-URN  = "URN:service:" service
service      = top-level *("." sub-service)
top-level    = let-dig [ *25let-dig-hyp let-dig ]
sub-service  = let-dig [ *let-dig-hyp let-dig ]

Top-level service names MUST NOT exceed 27 characters, so that they fit within S-NAPTR. There is no single global resolution service: each top-level service can provide its own mapping protocols. Validation, in the sense of checking that a string is a currently assigned URN, is not possible because not every mapping server knows every registration.
sections.eli5: A name is built like a family tree: "sos" is the whole family and "sos.fire" is one member. If you drop the last part, you get a more general name that still makes sense.

sections.title: The IANA Registry and Its Rules
sections.content:
Labels are managed by IANA in a new registry called "Service URN Labels". Creating a new top-level service requires the Standards Action policy. The policy for sub-services may differ for each top-level service and MUST be set by the document that describes that top-level service.

For sos, new sub-services need expert review. They must be of general public interest and of a similar emergency nature, offered widely in different countries with about the same caller expectation. The expert is designated by the ECRIT working group, its successor, or, in their absence, the IESG. The sos service is not meant for general government, public information, counseling or social services.

The counseling service covers advice and support, often anonymous, that does not require an emergency response. Its sub-services use expert review chosen in the same way.
sections.eli5: A librarian (IANA) keeps the official list of names. Adding a whole new category needs a formal standard, and adding a new emergency type needs an expert to agree it is a real, widespread emergency.

sections.title: The Services Defined Here
sections.content:
The initial registration defines two top-level services and their sub-services.

  • sos: emergency services. The generic urn:service:sos reaches a public safety answering point (PSAP), which dispatches appropriate aid. Sub-services are ambulance, animal-control, fire, gas, marine, mountain, physician, poison and police.
  • counseling: the generic service reaches a call center that transfers the caller by need. Sub-services are children, mental-health and suicide (the suicide prevention hotline).

The physician service connects the caller to a physician referral service, and poison refers to poison control centers.
sections.eli5: The list starts with two big groups: emergency help (fire, police, ambulance and more) and people to talk to when you need advice or support.

sections.title: Security and Alternatives Rejected
sections.content:
As an identifier, the URN raises no particular security issue, since services are meant to be well known. Carrying it in a signaling protocol, however, can tell an attacker what kind of service the caller wants, making it easier to find all calls for emergency services or directory assistance. Protocols carrying service URNs need their own appropriate security mechanisms. The mapping protocol must address the threats detailed in RFC 5069.

Appendix A explains why other designs were not chosen. tel:NNN;context=+C is hard for proxies because they would need to know every number-context pair, and numbers collide: 118 is an emergency number in Italy but reaches directory assistance in Finland. A tel:sos URI needs an extension to tel URIs. A sip:sos@domain user overloads the user part of the URI and is SIP-specific. A special domain would need one logical emergency proxy for the whole world, which scales poorly.
sections.eli5: Saying which kind of help you want could tell a snoop something about you, so the messages carrying it need protecting. Other naming ideas were tried and dropped because they clashed or were too hard to run.
